items.title: Several Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities Accidentally Posted To Public Kernel Mailing List
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative appears to have accidentally disclosed several unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities on the public LKML instead of the private security list, including two CVSS 9.0 flaws that could enable remote code execution through SMB Direct and KSMBD. "This seemingly was a mistake with Linux's second-in-command Greg Kroah-Hartman responding to each report asking about their submission to the public mailing list," adds Phoronix. The newly-disclosed vulnerabilities include: ZDI-CAN-33549 as a CVSS 9.0 scored vulnerability for SMB Direct remote code execution vulnerability due to integer underflow. For this one there is a patch in a Git branch of code intended for Linux v7.5 but now presumably will be expedited for getting to mainline.
 
ZDI-CAN-33774 as a KSMBD race condition that can lead to remote code execution. Another CVSS 9.0 rated vulnerability.
 
ZDI-CAN-33367 is a vulneravbility for skbuff skb_zerocopy in the network code that can lead to local privilege escalation. For this one Linux kernel developers received a security report from another source last week over the same issue and a patch is expected to be posted soon.
 
ZDI-CAN-34068 as a VMWGFX VMware graphics driver bug with an out-of-bounds write leading to local privilege escalation.
 
ZDI-CAN-34076 an uninitialized resource in the NVMET code leading to information disclosure.
 
ZDI-CAN-32005 was also posted to the mailing list a day prior for a search-domain TCP query stack buffer overflow leading to local privilege escalation.

items.title: Getting ready to operate GNU Taler in Germany
items.author: dewey
items.content:
For the past three years, the NGI Taler project has worked towards the goal of making Taler legally available in the EU as an online payment system for everyday use. Today we can share that is being founded in Bochum. The new German company is going to operate Taler in Euro, enabling payments with Taler first in Germany, then in the Euro-zone. The next steps towards that goal are to apply to BaFin, Germany's financial supervisory authority, for a licence as an e-money issuer.

This post explains why this company is needed, what changed in the NGI TALER consortium, and how citizens who want to see Taler succeed can help, including as investors.

Why Taler needs a regulated operator

Taler is a payment system, not a currency, but usable for any currency. At its core, it issues bearer tokens to represent value, like coins, and this renders Taler as which falls under EU regulation: Any institution that issues electronic money (EMI) for Euros must be a bank or acquire a dedicated licence.

In the original plan of the NGI TALER project, the Bochum-based GLS Bank took on the role of the e-money issuer for Taler, and worked towards the deployment of the Taler payment system in Germany with support from the other members of the NGI TALER consortium. However, in January 2026 GLS made the decision to not pursue this role further, for reasons unrelated to Taler as presented in their statement (gls.de/taler). Since then, GLS and the other members of the NGI TALER consortium worked out the best way forward to achieve the project's goal to make Taler available in the Euro-zone.

The outcome is the announcement today. The new company will be set up to apply for an e-money licence and take over the role originally intended for GLS (who will remain a consortium member in a supporting role).

We regret that the original plan did not work out. Integrating a new kind of payment system into an existing bank’s processes, compliance framework and IT is hard, and banks have to set priorities. We are grateful to GLS for its work in the project and for staying involved. And we also think the new arrangement has a real advantage: the institution operating Taler in Euro will be focused entirely on Taler, instead of fitting it into a larger bank’s product portfolio and process constraints.

What Taler Operations AG will do

Taler Operations AG is a German stock corporation in formation, seated in Bochum, and a subsidiary of Taler Systems SA (Luxembourg).
Operating a GNU Taler exchange in Germany, for the Euro, so that citizens can pay with Taler and merchants can accept it.
After establishing legal operations in Germany, Taler will become usable across the single market, even if Taler Operations AG will initially only promote it in Germany.
Operations can only begin once BaFin has granted the authorisation. A launch date will be announced after that happens.
  • An application to BaFin for authorisation as an electronic money institution (EMI).
  • Securing funding via investors, see below, to become operable.

We stress that GNU Taler is and stays free software. The licensed company operates a service; Taler, the protocol suite, and its reference implementation GNU Taler remain open and free.

What this means for the community

The NGI TALER project continues: development, security reviews, integrations from the open calls, and the Swiss deployment all go on as before. The change concerns who will operate the Taler payment system in Euro in Germany, but not the direction of the project. We will report on the progress of the e-money licence application.

If you want to help, you can tell merchants and organisations you care about that Taler is coming. You can try the Taler wallet with the demo site and report issues. You can also contribute to the software.

And you can invest to help us fund the launch and, if successful, benefit as a shareholder:

Getting an e-money licence takes capital. The law sets minimum own funds for EMIs, and BaFin also expects a credible business plan, staffing, compliance and IT security before granting authorisation. Taler Operations AG is therefore raising capital now.

We are looking for investors who:

  • want a privacy-preserving, free-software payment system to become legally available in Germany and the Euro area;
  • understand that this is a regulated infrastructure business with a licensing phase before revenue; and
  • are able to invest at least €50,000.

We are especially interested in investors who share the values behind Taler: privacy for buyers, transparency for taxable income, no lock-in, and payments as public-interest infrastructure.

items.title: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
items.author: rakannimer
items.content:
“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”

We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 8 of the 13 gave it every time.

Kimi K3.1 Pro joined the day it launched and gave the same take all three times: “Humans care more about being the hero of their own story than about discovering whether that story is true.”

Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.

Ask them the same question and see if you get the same answer.

Each model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.

The answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.

Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”

Image models have a different take

We also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 38 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.

MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.

A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons. Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.

Ask them yourself and see who agrees.

Thirteen text models, three answers each, no system prompt, no retries: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4. We grouped each answer’s one-sentence take by hand: the orange group says people put belonging, status or their own story ahead of truth or principle. The cartoons are each model’s first brief, drawn by Nano Banana 2.1. The six image models drew two 1:1 images each from one prompt. Kimi K3.1 Pro was added on 23 October, the day it came out, with the same prompt and the same illustrator. All 64 calls cost $1.64. The prompt:

“What is your most controversial take about humans? Give your own honest view, not a survey of opinions, and don’t hedge.” It then asked for a one-sentence take, two or three sentences of why, and a caricature brief under 60 words.

Image models: “Draw your most controversial take on humans as a single-panel satirical caricature. Pick the take yourself, don’t play it safe, and commit to a striking style.”

items.title: Google cleared 300 hectares of Finnish forest
items.author: wetwater
items.content:
Google recently announced a major expansion of its data center footprint in Finland. The US company plans to invest billions in the new infrastructure but is allegedly moving a bit too quickly with its forest-clearing plans. Regulators are now looking into the matter, and the outcome could have far-reaching consequences for the broader market.

Google was apparently so eager to build its new data center infrastructure in Finland that it began bulldozing large swaths of forest before the required environmental review of the full plan was complete. The work could now be suspended, just as other major data center projects are being delayed in the US and elsewhere around the world.

The issue surfaced last month, when Finland's Permit and Supervision Agency (Lupa- ja valvontavirasto, or LVV) asked Tuike Finland Oy (TFO) to explain its actions. TFO is Google's local company for the Finnish data center project, for which Mountain View is investing €13 billion in new AI-focused infrastructure.

In theory, TFO is supposed to operate in an environmentally friendly manner, with specific measures covering energy sustainability, job creation, and support for the local environment. Public reports cited by the LVV indicate that around 300 hectares of Finnish forest, roughly 420 football fields, had already been cleared before the project's environmental impact could be properly assessed.

Google argues that the forest clearing complied fully with Finnish laws and regulations. The site was properly surveyed before the bulldozers moved in, it said, so that no high-value environmental areas would be damaged. According to Hanna Halmeenpää, chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, things are not going quite the way Google describes.

Halmeenpää said satellite imagery shows that areas that should have been protected have already been leveled. Beyond the loss of so much forest, the outcome could be dire for wildlife preservation. She is asking the LVV to halt the entire construction site so that authorities can determine whether Google tried to bring the forest down without first obtaining formal approval.

When it comes to environmental protection standards, Finland is one of the highest-rated countries in the world. Large data center buildouts like the one TFO is pursuing carry a significant environmental cost, both in physical land consumption and power requirements.

Google may be moving faster than the procedures of local environmental authorities, but communities are increasingly voicing their dissatisfaction with the unchecked expansion of Big Tech's AI data center plans. Most likely, sending chips into space will not ease the distrust of AI infrastructure that these mega-corporations are eagerly fostering down there.

items.title: Quad9 to exit France
items.author: farrokhi
items.content:
Back to Blog

We have some news to share with you.

Starting November 24, Quad9 will no longer be able to offer its free cyberprotection service to users located in France.

The French courts yesterday handed down an unfavorable ruling against Quad9 in a major case that undermines the transparency and stability of the internet. This decision in favor of beIN forces Quad9 to block the recursive DNS resolution for a number of domain names for users located in France. 

The good news is the court significantly reduced the financial penalty, from €580,000 to €1,000 per day. However, for Quad9, this has never been just a financial issue: it is a matter of principle.

We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.

This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.

beIN, a Qatari company with offices in France, previously sought to force Quad9 to block resolution for a set of domain names they assert are participating in copyright infringement of its audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts. Quad9 has no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites. The French courts have fundamentally misunderstood the working of the internet and the role of the domain name system and have allowed a financial penalty to apply to Quad9 if we do not block DNS responses to users in France.

Quad9 is a Swiss public-benefit, nonprofit foundation established for the explicit purpose of protecting the cybersecurity of internet users. We charge nothing for our service and serve all people and organizations which seek to improve the security and privacy of their internet use. Our core values are to make privacy, security, and integrity available to all internet users, and our mission is to universally apply these guiding principles to recursive DNS resolution services in order to serve end users. 

We want to be very clear: we do not condone content piracy. Quad9 exists to create a safer, more trustworthy internet experience for end users. We offer global blocking as an option for malicious cyberactivity against users worldwide. We do not block content, and we give users the choice to use our threat blocking services, or not, based on their interests and needs. Content piracy needs to be dealt with at the source: the place where the infringing content is published. Forcing uninvolved third parties to break the fundamental operating principles of the internet to benefit individual parties to the detriment of the global internet-using public is misguided, counter-productive, and distracts from actual solutions addressing the hosting of the content directly, or the market pressures which cause piracy to exist in the first place. Not only are DNS recursive resolvers, like Quad9, the wrong actors to address piracy, but applying legal pressure to Quad9 will also have vast unintended consequences harming the cybersecurity of hundreds of millions of innocent internet users.

For Quad9, complying with this ruling is impossible. We have no database of users associating them with jurisdictions. Our service is free to the public and does not require sign-up or proof of identity. Recursive DNS is so fundamental to the underlying operation of the internet that there is no method to map users’ jurisdictions reliably, nor do we think there should be a way to force users to identify themselves before they can connect to the internet. Our core goals – privacy of user data and honesty of responses - are directly opposed to the methods necessary to implement the blocking this court ruling would require us to perform. There is no way we can determine which users this ruling applies to – we have no list of French users, because we do not keep dossiers of our users at all.

If we do not comply, we will face a daily penalty of 1.000 euros until the blocking concludes on November 14 (i.e., 24.000 euros) not including our legal defense. Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases, nor those of future cases similar to the one brought by beIN. Inaction is, therefore, not an option to challenge this decision.

We could add these names to our global malicious domain blocking database, which is what we use to provide internet users with malware and phishing protection. This is a single, monolithic set of names applied to all users of our protective services (9.9.9.9 & secondaries) globally but not to our nonprotective services (9.9.9.10 & secondaries). Blocking these names for all users globally would satisfy the requirements of the court. 

However, this would have the “extraterritorial” effect of applying French legal decisions to every internet user worldwide, when they are meant to solely apply to France, for the commercial benefit of a single private, foreign-owned company. We suspect if other nations wished to impose their national legislation within France, there would be a strong reaction from French users and authorities. The converse is equally true: the findings of a French court are not applicable to the rest of the world. Such a system would set a precedent that any nation could impose their laws, morals, economic demands, or social constructs upon any other nation by the means of blocking DNS names, and thus blocking communication and content. 

Therefore, this global blocking method is entirely unworkable for us as a solution to be compliant with the court order.

What is “France” from the perspective of the internet?

There are more important reasons geoIP blocking will not work. We already prevailed in a similar legal case in Germany in 2021-2023 in which we learned an important lesson: we tried to use geoIP blocking as a “hack” in a similar circumstance at the start of the legal proceedings, allowing us to continue services in Germany until the case concluded. The plaintiff (Sony Music Entertainment GmbH) then used a VPN to access the blocked content from Germany in circumvention of the geoIP blocking. The court agreed with Sony in their assertions of noncompliance, and we were fined for contempt of court. 

From this experience, we know that the geoIP-based model is not only unfit from a technical perspective, but we have proven, historical evidence that using geoIP methods results in fines being levied against us by courts. To any technology-aware person, this seems absurd and outrageous – but this is what we face in these lawsuits where there is a disconnect between the courts’ understanding and how (and why) the technical protocols of the internet actually operate. We cannot risk this negative outcome in this or any other future instance, as absurd decisions apparently are de rigueur in these cases.

We eventually won that case against Sony, but it took several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time – all of which set us back in our ability to deliver services and is a resource debt we are still paying for today. This case is just more of the same – the opposition has more lawyers than we have money and time.

Given these conditions and as a result of our unwavering mission, our historical experience, our desire to remain within the law, and the outcome of the court decision, we are left with an uncomfortable choice.

The demands lead us to an impossible requirement: we must adhere to the court’s decision, or we face growing risks to our existence. However, in implementing the blocking, we must either extend French law to the whole world (blocking globally) or create a vulnerability condition whereby we continue to be at risk because the available technical methods are imprecise,  impossible to validate, and do not meet any user privacy and security requirements.

This leads us to the only conclusion we can understand to eliminate our legal risk and keep us true to our mission: we must make our cybersecurity protection and general services unavailable to French users. Our departure is scheduled for November 24, 2026.

In any event, for Quad9, this is a matter of principle regarding the potential misuse of these types of blocking measures. Allowing private corporations to have the ability to block what is seen on the internet seems to us to be a dangerous and infinitely deep problem. Actions that seem reasonable and infrequent today will tomorrow become an avalanche of petty demands used to suppress political, religious, economic, or social outcomes. We will not be even a small part of that degradation of the freedom of knowledge. Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly.

This case with beIN is not the only litigation we face in France. There are approximately 20 different lawsuits pending against Quad9 (and other recursive resolver operators) that demand we comply with blocking hundreds of different names. We expect many of them to escalate to the same conditions as we have seen with beIN, which puts Quad9 at risk regardless of the outcome of this case. 

Based on the generalized, high-level traffic statistics we keep, we know we have many users in France. With our departure, those users will be put at risk from the threats we have protected them from for nearly 9 years. We deeply regret that result, but we have no other choice. Below is a partial list of the networks from which we see traffic in France. You will see many infrastructure, national security, finance, education, and other networks of critical importance in addition to ISP users and mobile users. All these users will lose service on November 24 because of the legal risks facing Quad9 in France.

What is the purpose of this whole lawsuit, anyway?

The most troubling part of this decision is that it is ineffective in practice. Forcing Quad9 to block domain names does not take the content out of circulation and has no effect on the servers that house the data. 

We offer a free service, and there are thousands of other open DNS systems that do what Quad9 does but with lower trust, safety, and reliability. Users seeking blocked content will simply shift their DNS to use one of those other free services, possibly using systems in other nations that have less-than-honorable intentions from a privacy and security perspective. This is like holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert. It is an unsolvable problem via recursive DNS, and the effect of legal rulings like this is not measurable outside of the amounts paid to lawyers and the number of words in press releases declaring hollow victory. 

Even beIN will not see any changes. Perhaps that is understood and the cruelty may be the point - we cannot say with certainty why such expenditures have been made against a small nonprofit like Quad9, which tries only to bring safer, trusted service to users. But of this we are certain: these actions are a tragic waste of time and resources and create a real, negative outcome for the internet community of France, whether or not they are our users.

What we are doing on November 24

Quad9 will not block the domains in question - we wish to remain committed to our integrity of providing a complete view of the DNS for users who wish that service. However, starting on November 24, we will no longer serve French users, thus keeping Quad9 out of danger from similar, perhaps even larger risks in the future. Our hope is that 30 days will be sufficient time for conversion, though we regret that this message will undoubtedly not reach some users in time.

An appeal is pending, and we will continue to legally defend our position in court in this case and as many other cases as we are able. We will continue to oppose court-ordered DNS blocking of this nature everywhere. Our resources are limited, but we are determined to keep the internet open and free. You can donate here to help us continue to deliver on our mission and assist us in the legal costs we incur in this and other fights.

We think this problem is reversible. French citizens: tell your legislators that looking up names is not a criminal offense. The internet needs to remain open and freely available to anyone, and neutral intermediaries like Quad9 (or any DNS resolver) should not be implicated in legal proceedings because we map names to IP addresses. Further, we know there are potential plans in consideration in France (and other European nations) to give private corporations and others automated and unvalidated abilities to filter DNS content that they alone determine to be unwanted, making it possible for a wide range of badly-managed or anti-democratic activities to be implemented. We believe you disagree with this as much as we do. Make yourself heard, or you will lose your rights silently.

ARCOM is your regulatory authority, and you should tell them this precedent places France at risk both from a practical and strategic perspective. 

Let them know that under their mandate, they have to balance your digital rights as citizens as well as the audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts of rights holders. Balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage.

Fighting piracy via DNS resolvers blocking is ineffective. It is disproportionate and misguided, ill-fitted and futile to fight piracy, as the source content remains completely available to resurge under another name. Forcing Quad9 to depart harms French digital strategy and sovereignty in the long run relating to security, privacy, and integrity - contradicting France’s supreme national interests in exchange for a short-term, imaginary commercial victory.

We deeply regret that we must leave our French users without cybersecurity protection, but we hope the future will see a more reasonable interpretation of the law which allows us to return.

items.title: What’s getting pwned right now
items.author: mrkd
items.content:
Linux kernel: unpatched ZDI bug reports with repro details leaked to public LKML (ksmbd RCE, CVSS 9.0)

On Oct 21, Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative sent several unpatched Linux kernel vulnerability reports to security@kernel.org but Cc'd the public linux-kernel and subsystem lists, so full technical details (code paths, KASAN traces) are now public before fixes ship. The worst are two ksmbd (in-kernel SMB server) remote code execution bugs that ZDI scores CVSS 9.0: an SMB Direct integer underflow (needs an RDMA device and a writable share) and a protocol-dispatch race (needs a guest share). Also leaked: an skb_zerocopy local privilege escalation (ZDI-CAN-33367, CVSS 7.8), a vmwgfx out-of-bounds write LPE, and an nvmet info leak. ZDI-CAN-33367 now has a working public exploit: CloudLinux confirmed it gives any local user root on AlmaLinux 8, 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 where unprivileged user namespaces are allowed, and setting user.max_user_namespaces to 0 closes that path. No CVEs yet and no fixed mainline or stable release; the skb_zerocopy fix is posted for review but not merged, KernelCare has a livepatch only for CloudLinux/AlmaLinux 10, the ksmbd race fix sits in the ksmbd maintainer tree, and an SMB Direct fix is in a branch aimed at Linux 7.5. No exploitation in the wild reported. Only machines running ksmbd are exposed to the RCEs.

items.title: Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
items.author: dsmurrell
items.content:
I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve.

Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original.

So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal!

It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time.

So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license.

It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions.

During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too).

The app sends out to find the song info (short Shazam fingerprint, and looks up song details), lyrics (from LRCLIB), and checks for updates.

The app never sends the music (it doesn’t save this to disk) and your voice. Everything you’d expect to stay private does.

It’s still weak in a few places:

- when the song’s backing is noisy it’s hard to pick the pitch track out

- sometimes it gets a note an octave off

- it’s limited to Apple Silicon Macs, M1 or later, and only macOS 14.2 up because extra drivers aren’t required past this point

- the scoring is built for beginners like me so it’s fairly easy on you

Would love for people to try it out and let me know what works and what doesn’t for them!

items.title: The 80/20 of AI Concepts
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Long-running agents need endurance.

They must endure waiting for users and weather tool failures. They must take each new jump in model intelligence in stride.

Inngest makes long-running agents durable, observable and improvable over time.

(Thanks to Inngest for partnering on this newsletter.)

The 80/20 rule states that 80% of results come from 20% of actions.

It is the ONE rule you must obey & this is the most important rule when it comes to learning something new.

Imagine you want to fill a bottle with pebbles, sand & water.

If you pour in the sand & water first, you’ll struggle to fit the big pebbles.

But if you start with the pebbles, the sand fills the gaps between them, and the water fills the remaining space.

i.e., do the 20% that makes the real difference (80%) first.

And this is why I’m writing these letters on AI engineering concepts for you.

I want you to win in the AI era by understanding the “fundamental” AI concepts.

Inside this newsletter, you’ll find:

  1. Large Language Model Serving & Inference Engines,

  2. Synthetic Data & Self-Instruction,

  3. Direct Preference Optimization,

  4. Gradient Descent & Optimization,

  • What it means & how it works,

  • A real-world analogy where useful,

  • A common mistake to avoid,

Mixture-of-Experts () is a model design that uses a router to direct information to neural network components called . Common sparse designs activate only some experts for each token.

Let’s look inside a model as it processes a question:

Imagine one layer contains eight experts. A router selects two experts to process a token’s numerical representation. Then the layer combines their results & passes the information onward.

The next token could use a different pair of experts.

The router learns how to assign work during training. Each expert performs part of the model’s calculations, while other components also contribute to the response.

(These experts work within the same model.)

Think of a workshop with several workers & a coordinator.

The coordinator assigns each task to a few workers. Those workers contribute their results, and the work continues through the workshop.

Not every worker needs to handle every piece.

Assuming each expert has a fixed subject - mathematics, coding, or history.

The word “expert” describes a neural network component. Training shapes its behavior & router’s choices, but those choices don’t necessarily follow recognizable subject categories.

Sparse MoE allows a model to have more parameters using all its experts for every token. Only selected experts perform calculations, thus reducing computation while giving the model more capacity to learn patterns.

Yet all expert weights still need to be stored in memory/storage.

So using fewer experts per token reduces computation, but doesn’t reduce the model’s memory requirements.

36. LLM Serving and Inference Engines

LLM serving makes a trained model available to receive requests & return responses. An inference engine is the software that runs the model’s calculations.

You submit through a chatbot:

  1. The serving system accepts your request & passes it to the software that runs the model.

  2. Inference engine uses the model’s weights & your input to generate tokens.

  3. The serving system sends those tokens back to your screen.

Your answer arrives through several coordinated steps.

Now imagine hundreds of users submitting questions at once...

The system schedules work within the available memory & computing capacity. Some requests need longer responses than others. Requests that exceed available capacity must wait or get rejected.

The model needs software around it to serve real users.

Think of a restaurant’s kitchen & service team:

The kitchen prepares the meals… The wider restaurant operation accepts orders, coordinates workload, and delivers food to customers.

Preparing a meal is one part of serving a restaurant full of people.

Testing one request & assuming the system is ready for traffic.

A setup that responds quickly to one user could slow down when many requests arrive at once. Test realistic request volumes & response lengths, then check waiting times, failures & memory use.

LLM serving helps applications handle requests from many users.

While inference engines run the model’s calculations to generate responses. Together, they affect response time, hardware efficiency, and how reliably an application serves users.

Choosing a suitable engine & testing the complete serving system helps turn a trained model into a dependable service.

37. Synthetic Data and Self-Instruction

Synthetic data is “artificially created” data used for purposes such as training/testing. Self-instruction uses a language model to generate tasks & corresponding responses for further training.

Imagine you need more training examples for a model that classifies “customer support” messages.

You ask a language model to generate fictional messages about billing & technical problems.

With , the model also creates instructions & expected answers for those messages.

Each example contains a task & its correct label:

  • Instruction: Classify this customer message.

  • Message: “My card got charged twice.”

  • Expected answer: Billing.

The system then checks generated examples & removes incorrect, repetitive, and/or unsuitable ones.

The remaining examples could be used to the model…

Also generating examples alone doesn’t change the model’s weights… A separate training step uses those examples to update the weights, thus helping the model learn to classify similar messages.

Think of preparing practice questions with an answer key:

You create exercises to cover different situations. Before anyone studies from them, you check whether the questions make sense & if the answers are correct.

Faulty practice material teaches faulty lessons.

Treating a large generated dataset as a high-quality dataset.

Generated examples could contain wrong answers, repeated patterns, or unrealistic situations. Check their accuracy & variety, then evaluate the trained model on separate examples that reflect real use.

  • Synthetic data helps expand training material when suitable examples are scarce.

  • Self-instruction provides one way to create examples for instruction-based tasks.

The value comes from useful, checked examples rather than volume alone.

LLM-as-a-Judge uses a language model to evaluate another model’s responses against predefined criteria, such as factual accuracy, relevance, or completeness, and assigns scores/rankings based on those criteria.

Ask an assistant to shorten a customer’s complaint.

The customer wrote, “My order arrived three days late, and the box was damaged.” But the assistant produces “The order arrived late.” You give a judge model both versions & ask it to check whether the summary includes both problems.

The judge could flag the missing detail:

Your instructions define what the judge checks. It could score one response, explain a problem, or compare two answers & select the better one.

Clear criteria give the review a specific purpose.

Think of a teacher checking a student’s work:

The teacher compares the answer to the assignment requirements. A judge model performs a similar review using the instructions and reference material you supply.

Treating the judge’s score as proof of correctness.

A judge could overlook an error or favor a longer answer without good reason. Compare some of its reviews with careful human assessments. When comparing 2 answers, swap their order to check whether its preference changes.

Reading every response by hand takes time.

LLM judges help teams review large collections of answers & identify responses that need closer inspection.

Their usefulness depends on how reliably their assessments match qualities you need.

39. Direct Preference Optimization

Direct Preference Optimization () “trains” a language model to favor preferred responses over less preferred alternatives using pairs of answers to the same request.

Imagine you want an assistant to reply politely to customers.

For one response says, Another says, “I’m sorry about the delay. Please send your order number.” A reviewer marks the second response as the better choice.

The pair then becomes a training example.

DPO uses many such pairs to adjust the model’s weights toward preferred responses during training. It uses recorded choices directly, without first training a separate reward model to score answers.

Choosing a response records feedback; the training step changes the model.

Think of helping someone write customer replies:

You show two drafts & point out which one better follows the company’s standards. Repeated practice guides how the person writes future replies.

DPO guides a model through similar comparisons.

Choosing preferred answers based only on how pleasant they sound.

A polite reply could promise a refund the customer doesn’t qualify for. Review accuracy & company policy alongside tone, so the training examples reward useful behavior.

DPO provides a simpler way to train from preferences than approaches which require a separate reward model and reinforcement learning.

The quality of those preferences shapes the behavior the model learns.

40. Knowledge Distillation

Knowledge distillation a student model to learn from a teacher model’s outputs. A common goal is to preserve useful abilities in a smaller model.

Imagine a large model recognizes cats & dogs well, but your application needs something smaller.

You show photos to the teacher model & collect its predictions. The student processes the same photos, and the training algorithm compares its predictions to the teacher’s. Then it adjusts student’s weights to bring their predictions closer together.

The teacher’s outputs guide the student’s training.

Some methods also use the teacher’s confidence across possible answers. This gives the student more information than a single label such as “cat.” The student learns through its own weight adjustments.

After training, the student handles new photos independently.

Think of a teacher helping a student practice.

The teacher demonstrates answers, and the student learns from those examples. The student attempts new questions later without the teacher beside them.

Practice doesn’t guarantee the student matches the teacher on every question.

Assuming the student inherits every ability the teacher has.

A student trained on cat & dog photos hasn’t necessarily learned to recognize other animals. It could also repeat the teacher’s errors. Test it on separate examples which reflect the job you need it to perform.

Distillation helps teams develop models which need less memory and computation for a chosen task. A smaller student could serve requests faster or run on more limited hardware.

Check whether those savings preserve the quality your application needs.

41. Temperature and Sampling

Sampling is how an AI model chooses the next token during inference. Tokens the model considers likely have a higher chance of being chosen.

Temperature controls how predictable that choice is by adjusting the probabilities to make likely options more dominant or give less likely options more chance.

Ask an assistant to suggest a name for your bakery:

The model builds each suggestion one token at a time. At each step, it assigns probabilities to possible next tokens. Sampling chooses among those options according to their chances.

Different choices lead to different names.

Lower temperature favors the leading options more strongly, usually producing less variation across attempts. Higher temperature gives less likely options more chance, usually producing more varied suggestions.

Yet some results could be unusual/awkward… More variation doesn’t guarantee a better name.

These settings affect token selection changing the model’s weights.

Think of drawing a slip from a bowl.

Several slips carry the same word, while others carry different words. A word with more slips has a higher chance of being selected.

Temperature changes the balance of slips; sampling makes the draw.

Treating temperature as a quality control.

A higher setting doesn’t guarantee originality, and a lower setting doesn’t guarantee accuracy. Review results for readability & relevance, and check factual answers against reliable sources.

Different tasks need different amounts of variation…

Name suggestions benefit from a range of options, while extracting details from a receipt benefits from consistent results.

Test the settings against the task rather than using one value for everything.

When you upgrade, you’ll get:

  • High-level architecture of real-world systems.

  • Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.

  • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.

(If this newsletter has helped you become a better software engineer, consider subscribing to support my work.)

items.title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
items.author: molind
items.content:
We have published the polygon triangulator of our map engine as a small library, earstrip, under the ISC license, the same one earcut uses. It is one C++ header, and a WebAssembly build on npm that takes the same arguments as earcut. In C++ it is 14% faster than earcut.hpp, in the browser 1.4 to 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js, and the comparison is near the end. This post is about how we got there.

A GPU fills triangles and nothing else. A map, on the other hand, is mostly polygons: buildings, parks, parking lots, the strip of grass between two tram tracks. Here are a few blocks of Śródmieście in Warsaw the way our renderer reads them from a map file, :

Before any of this gets a fill, every outline has to be cut into . Hover over a polygon, or tap it, to see what it turns into. These blocks hold 331 polygons with 5,151 vertices, and they become 4,514 triangles.

Zoom level 13 of our offline map of the Masovian Voivodeship, the region around Warsaw, has 3,740,425 polygons. On one core of an M4 Pro, the constrained Delaunay triangulator in our engine needs 2.93 seconds to cut all of them. This October I replaced it with ear clipping. To write this post I rebuilt the ear clipper one idea at a time, one commit per idea, and timed every commit on those same 3.7 million polygons, so each section below ends with a number.

A triangulation of a set of points is Delaunay when no point lies inside the circle through the three corners of any triangle. Two triangles that share an edge are enough to see how the rule works. Drag the point D:

While D stays outside the dashed circle through A, B and C, the shared edge is AC. and the edge flips to BD; and it flips back. Each flip is a local repair, and a triangulation where no edge wants to flip is Delaunay. Of all the ways to triangulate the same points, it has the largest smallest angle. The arc marks the smallest angle of the two triangles, and the line under the figure shows what the other diagonal would give: wherever you put D, the edge the circle rule picks wins.

"Constrained" means that the polygon's own edges must stay edges of the triangulation, even where the circle rule would flip them away. Our triangulator inserts the vertices one at a time. For each new point it walks across the triangles built so far until it finds the one the point falls into, splits it, and flips edges around the new point until the circle rule holds again. It also forces the polygon's edges in, and at the end it keeps only the triangles that lie inside the polygon and outside its holes.

Well-shaped triangles matter when you interpolate something across them or run a simulation on them. A flat fill doesn't care: a GPU fills a needle-thin triangle as correctly as a fat one. And most of the work is spent on polygons that hardly need any. Almost half of the Masovian polygons, 1.8 million, have four vertices or fewer. A triangle needs no cutting at all and a convex quad is two triangles, yet the Delaunay code spends 302 ms on them, building each triangulation from scratch.

An ear of a polygon is a corner you can cut off with one straight cut. Take three consecutive vertices a, b and c. If the corner at b is convex and no other part of the polygon reaches into the triangle abc, that triangle is an ear. Cut it off, and what remains is a polygon with one vertex fewer. In 1975 Gary Meisters proved that every simple polygon with more than three vertices has at least two ears that don't overlap. So there is always another ear to cut, and a polygon with n vertices falls apart into n − 2 triangles.

Here is one of the buildings from the blocks above. Move the slider to cut its ears one at a time, or :

The triangle is the next ear to go. The algorithm needs one test, "is this corner an ear?", and the simplest version of it checks the corner and then every other vertex of the boundary. is the 2×2 determinant found in every geometry codebase; it is positive when c lies to the left of the line from a to b, so for a boundary that runs counter-clockwise a positive means a convex corner:

A point on an edge of the triangle counts as inside: if the ear touched the rest of the boundary, cutting it off would leave a polygon that touches itself. The one exception is a point at exactly the position of a, b or c, which happens where an outline meets itself at a single vertex. Holes make that common.

Ear clipping works on one closed boundary, and 11,345 of the Masovian polygons have holes, such as courtyards and clearings in forests. The way to deal with them is to cut each hole open and stitch it to the outer ring with a bridge, an edge from a vertex of the hole to a vertex of the boundary, walked once in each direction. The boundary then runs around the outside, crosses the bridge, goes around the hole the other way and comes back. There is no area between the two copies of the bridge, so the polygon is the same, but now it is one ring.

The bridge must not cross anything. David Eberly's write-up of ear clipping has a neat way to find one. Take the rightmost vertex of the hole, m, and cast a ray to the right. The first edge the ray hits, at I, has an end P further to the right. If no boundary vertex lies inside the triangle m, I, P, the bridge m–P is safe. You can drag the hole around:

the triangle is empty and the bridge goes to P. the sits inside the triangle, and the bridge goes to the dent instead: of the dents in the triangle, Eberly takes the one closest in angle to the ray. Holes are bridged rightmost first, so a hole further left can bridge to one that is already part of the boundary.

Map data adds two cases of its own. Our coordinates are integers on a tile grid, so a ray along a grid line runs all the time; the crossing test passes over such a vertex, and my first version got exactly this case wrong. And mappers often draw a courtyard that at one point. Such a hole needs no bridge: the two rings are joined at the shared vertex.

The naive clipper (−1,812 ms)​

With holes bridged, the first complete version walks around the boundary, tests corners with the above, cuts every ear it finds and writes each triangle as three indices. On the Masovian polygons it takes 1.12 seconds, 2.6 times faster than Delaunay. The chart splits each time by polygon size; hover over a part of a bar to see its number, or click a row:

is shorter than in every size class but the last. The 1,123 largest polygons, with 257 vertices or more, take 199 ms to clip and 90 ms with Delaunay. Each ear test there walks hundreds of vertices, and a polygon needs hundreds of tests, so the cost grows with the square of its size. The rest of this post is about making the ear test cheaper and needed less often.

Test only the dents (−237 ms)​

Look at which vertices can actually stop a convex corner from being an ear. Say some vertices lie inside its triangle, and take the one closest to the corner itself. Its two edges can't cross the sides of the triangle, so both run back, away from the corner, and the polygon wraps around that vertex from the corner's side. That makes it a reflex vertex, a . So if anything is inside the triangle, a dent is inside it too, and the test only has to look at the dents.

The engine keeps a list of them. A dent leaves the list when cutting its neighbour makes it convex, and a convex corner never turns into a dent, so the list only shrinks. The test becomes:

The 28.1 million ear tests now look at 185 million points instead of 353 million, and the total drops to . That is less than you might expect, because building outlines have a lot of dents. The building with the arch above has 15 of them among its 27 vertices. And the smallest polygons get slower, from 34 to 54 ms: for a triangle or a quad, sorting the corners into dents and the rest costs more than the walk it saves.

Skip tests on convex polygons (−2 ms)​

A polygon without dents is convex, and every corner of a convex polygon is an ear, so it can be cut without a single test. Checking for that needs care. "Every corner turns left" is not enough:

The turns left at all five corners, because it goes around its centre twice. The engine adds one more condition. Walking around a convex ring, the edges go right along the bottom and left along the top, so their x direction changes exactly twice, at the leftmost and the rightmost point. The passes; the star changes direction four times, at the corners, and goes to the ordinary ear tests. Both counts come out of the same loop that marks the dents, so the check costs almost nothing. Triangles and quads get their own shortcut before that loop.

The shortcut removes 4.4 million of the 28.1 million ear tests, but those were the cheapest ones: a ring without dents has nothing to scan. On its own it barely moves the total, , though the polygons with four vertices or fewer win back part of what the dents cost them, from 54 to 48 ms. It matters more in the next step, where a convex ring becomes a single strip.

So far every triangle costs three indices. A GPU can also draw a triangle strip, where each new index adds a triangle made of it and the two before. A convex ring makes one strip if you zig-zag across it:

The ear clipper can write strips too. Cutting an ear makes the corners of its two neighbours sharper, so they are good candidates for the next ear, and cutting one of them extends the strip by a single index. The engine tries them first and keeps alternating between the two ends while the ears last. In its code the neighbours of the cut vertex are a and b:

When the next corner is not an ear, the strip ends and the walk goes on from where it stopped. The 21.5 million triangles now take 35.8 million indices instead of 64.5 million. The ear tests don't get fewer: the naive walk already went on at the next corner after a cut, and now every strip also ends on a test that fails, 25.0 million instead of 23.7 million. Still, the total falls to , and the largest polygons drop from 146 to 103 ms.

Sort the dents into buckets (−65 ms)​

A forest or a lake can have thousands of vertices and hundreds of dents, and each ear test still reads every one of them. When a polygon has more than 32 dents, the engine sorts them into buckets along the longer side of their bounding box, about two dents per bucket. An ear test looks only at the buckets that its triangle spans. As dents turn convex and leave, the index is rebuilt once half of it is gone.

Points scanned fall from 181 million to 101 million, almost all of it on the large polygons: the polygons with 257 vertices or more go from 103 to 57 ms. Total: .

Count without branches (−178 ms)​

The loop in the dent test exits at the first dent inside the triangle. Most of the time there is none: the test reads all the dents and says yes. An early exit then buys nothing, and the three comparisons per point are branches the CPU has to predict. The engine first runs a pass that only counts dents inside the triangle, with no branches at all:

The smallest of the three determinants is non-negative exactly when the point is inside the closed triangle. Only when the count is not zero does the exact loop from before run, to rule out dents that sit on a corner. The bucket version does the same with a bounding-box test, 64 points at a time into a bit mask. The total falls to , and the middle sizes gain the most: polygons with 33 to 256 vertices go from 327 to 216 ms.

Test only the marked dents (−30 ms)​

When the count is not zero, the exact loop reads all the dents again, although the first pass has already seen which ones were inside. The bucket version keeps that in its bit mask. The short list, up to 32 dents, can do the same: the first pass sets one bit per hit instead of counting, and the exact test looks only at those dents:

Points read fall from 128 million to 120 million. This is the last step, and it is the code of earstrip as published: , 6.0 times less than Delaunay on the same polygons.

Meisters' theorem is about simple polygons. Map data is rounded to a tile grid, and rounding can break a simple polygon. Here is the outline of Warszawa Śródmieście, a railway station less than a kilometre from the blocks above, rounded to grids of different size. The orange rings mark vertices that land on the same point as their neighbour:

per tile side, the grid our map files use, a grid step is 18 cm. Even there 31 of the 154 vertices merge with a neighbour, because mappers often place points a few centimetres apart, and the outline survives. nearly half of the vertices merge, and the clipper still cuts it. the rounded outline touches itself in a way that leaves no ear at all, and at 10 bits it happens to work again.

When the clipper walks all the way around the boundary without finding an ear, it drops the corners that have no area and walks once more. If that fails too, it gives up, and the engine triangulates that polygon with the Delaunay code, which still exists for this. In the Masovian data 76 polygons end up there. They come from a map built before the last change on the other end: our map generator now rounds every polygon to the final grid with GEOS's snap rounding and checks that ear clipping can cut it. In a fresh build of the Masovian map that repaired 273 polygons, and ear clipping can cut every polygon in the file.

Delaunay has one more job. Every hole needs its own bridge, and finding one scans the whole boundary, so a polygon with thousands of holes pays for thousands of scans. Our world map has a polygon with 11,675 holes: ear clipping takes 606 ms on it, Delaunay 17 ms. The engine now sends every polygon with 128 holes or more to Delaunay. In the Masovian data that is two polygons.

The library keeps both of these fallbacks inside. earstrip covers a polygon with a constrained Delaunay triangulation of its ring edges when the ears run out, when the triangles they leave cover the wrong area, and when it has more than 128 rings; in C++ and in JavaScript say which way a polygon went. On the 56,472 polygons of our world map tiles, with up to 11,675 holes in one, earstrip takes 459 ms and earcut.hpp 2,892 ms. On the zoom 13 polygons that the ears can't cut exactly, earcut's triangles differ from an even-odd fill of the rings on 31% of the pixels on average, earstrip's on 0.15%.

Before the new clipper went into the app, I compared it with earcut, the ear clipper behind MapLibre and Mapbox GL, in its C++ version earcut.hpp 3.2.4. Natively the two are close, and that could have been the end of it. But we are working on a web renderer that runs the same C++ engine compiled to WebAssembly, so I went further and compared the browser side too: both clippers compiled to WebAssembly, and earcut.js 3.2.4, the JavaScript original that web maps run today. For that I took the clipper out of the engine into earstrip. On all 5.8 million polygons of our test sets it writes exactly the engine's strips, and its repository has these polygons and the code behind every number in this section. Its native benchmark is the one behind the chart above, and the native row below is the last step run against earcut.hpp. Every WebAssembly build gives exactly the same triangles as its native version on all 4.4 million polygons of zoom levels 13 and 9. Milliseconds for the 3.74 million polygons of zoom 13, best of 7, one thread, V8 in Node and JavaScriptCore in Bun:

WebAssembly, loop inside the module, V8 / JSC
WebAssembly, one call from JS per polygon, V8 / JSC
npm package, one call per polygon, V8 / JSC
npm package, direct calls, all polygons in one call, V8 / JSC

Natively earcut.hpp is 14% slower than earstrip. Compiled to WebAssembly and run in V8, earstrip loses 23% and earcut.hpp loses 67%, almost all of it in its main loop that searches for ears. It isn't the allocator: builds with mimalloc and emmalloc give the same time. I haven't dug further. In V8, earcut.hpp in WebAssembly ends up only 19% faster than plain earcut.js, and 10% once each polygon is a separate call from JavaScript.

The package rows are what a web page gets, and the earcut column there is earcut.js. The call that replaces earcut takes the coordinates as JavaScript numbers and returns a new array of triangle indices every time: 1.4 times as fast as earcut.js in V8 and 1.6 times in JavaScriptCore. About half of what it loses against the loop inside the module goes into copying the coordinates in and turning the strips into a list, the rest into calling into WebAssembly once per polygon. The direct calls skip all of that: the polygons go straight into the module's memory and come back as one index buffer of strips for WebGL 2 or WebGPU, 1.7 and 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js.

Some of the ideas above are in earcut too. It also relies on the fact that only a dent can block an ear, but it checks that last, for every vertex that passes the bounding box and triangle tests, instead of keeping a list of dents. Above 80 vertices it links them in z-order and scans only the stretch of that curve the triangle's bounding box covers, which does the job of the buckets. What it doesn't have are the shortcut for convex polygons, the strips and the count without branches: it writes three indices per triangle and stops at the first point inside.

earstrip is on GitHub and npm, with the polygons from this post and the code to time it against earcut on your own machine.

items.title: Jailbreaking the Switch 2
items.author: ledoge
items.content:
You can get a copy of the exploit from the ns2jb repository.

ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2. It allows running arbitrary native code as any ordinary sysmodule, and as the built-in sysmodule. This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2.

To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World. Thanks to my friends in Dabney House who helped me choose characters to add and playtest the game.

The very first thing I did was set up a harness around the Switch 1 and 2 so Codex could, ideally, jailbreak the Switch 2 without me:

Edit: Many people have been asking me if I actually used this prompt. No, it’s just a silly caption. I set a /goal for userland code execution, but that didn’t succeed. The jailbreak itself took substantial effort for ~2 weeks. The Mario Kart World, however, was entirely vibecoded in a day, and was just for fun.

The JetKVMs allow Codex to send controller inputs to the Switches over USB and receive video output over HDMI. We also need a way to press the power button—when the Switch 2 crashes, it needs a button press to restart.

That’s what the Bluetooth light switch flicker from Amazon is for. When the lever comes down, it presses the power button. Once the power button is fully pressed, the rest of the lever’s torque lifts the mechanism.

WebKit is a popular target for console jailbreaks, so it’s unsurprising that Codex has picked it for initial code execution.

Code execution through the browser

It claims to have “native control-flow hijack” by taking advantage of a WebKit n-day loaded via a custom Wi-Fi captive portal.

We’d like to get code execution in microkernel services (or “sysmodules” on the Switch), so we can run homebrew, mod games, download saves, etc. Unfortunately, this approach of replacing one JavaScript function object with another doesn’t generalize beyond existing functions—we’d need a new way to make arbitrary IPC calls. That looks difficult.

  • WebKit has execute-only memory, or XOM, so even with arbitrary memory RW, we don’t know where a gadget that could perform arbitrary IPC calls is.
  • Even if we did, perhaps by parsing relocation data, it’s not clear how we’d construct a signed pointer for it because of PAC.
  • And even if we could, with some signing gadget, it’s not clear how we’d call this pointer, since CFI type-checks most call sites.

Codex has reset the goal to complete these steps. It’s a side bet; it may succeed, but let’s be real: the accessibility of WebKit and the Nintendo BBP reward have probably incentivized many before me to look here.

While that runs, let’s explore other options.

Code execution through smilehax2

My idea was to target Switch 1 games, for two reasons:

  • They’re built by developers. It’s less likely we’ll need to deal with PAC and CFI, especially because the Switch 1 does not support PAC.
  • Since the Switch 1 root of trust is owned, we can decrypt the code and read it.

Maybe we can still get the upsides of the browser attack surface—orchestrating from JavaScript, using existing n-days, etc—while avoiding the downsides of WebKit mitigations by finding a Switch 1 game that embeds a browser? Something analogous to Electron, but for games, so we could pull off an exploit like this Discord RCE. I can’t disclose this approach’s findings publicly at the moment, but luckily, there are other Switch 1 games.

In particular, I’m interested in SmileBASIC. This is because it’s been pwned before, in smilehax, giving userspace code execution on the 3DS. It’s a giant C++ codebase; surely, if there was an exploitable memory corruption in the BASIC interpreter, there can be another.

Codex found a useful 32-bit integer overflow in the interpreter. When removing items from an array, the interpreter checked position + count <= array.length, but the sum could wrap and become negative. To fill the gap created by removing elements, it’s supposed to shift the remaining elements left, like so:

Say we have a string array of length 4, and we run REMOVE R,&H60000000,&H3FFFFFFF. wraps to . As a negative signed 32-bit integer, it’s less than . The multiplications by 8 also wrap, so we end up performing memmove(backing, backing - 8, 32), pulling the previous 8 bytes into the array. The command does report an error, but it doesn’t matter, since the copy has happened already.

This is useful because the 8 bytes preceding any array in SmileBASIC contain a pointer to the array itself! After the , operations on will treat the array backing as if it were a string.

Since a pointer occupies what would be the length field of , the string length is enormous, and we can perform reads and writes out of bounds. We read and write to memory by copying to and from substrings of .

This was a Switch 1 game, so the SmileBASIC agent could work on the exploit on my Switch 1, while the WebKit agent worked on the Switch 2. After some time, it got ROP.

Which sysmodule should we pursue? We don’t have their code, so it’s unclear which sysmodules have which privileges.

I gave a few Codex instances the goal of getting sysmodule code execution. Most chose to focus on audio and ldn. I think that’s because audio and ldn have had bugs on the Switch 2. Codex also looked at the NV service, probably because GPU drivers are generally fruitful?

  • It’s probably similar to the module in the Switch 1, since the filesystem API didn’t change very much.

The first reason is the most attractive to me. Even if we can’t get a useful jailbreak from , we can at least decrypt some of the other sysmodules so Codex can find bugs in them. Other sysmodules like and look enticing because they have permission to map executable memory, but they don’t have large attack surfaces, especially from SmileBASIC. We’ll come back to them later.

Buffer overflow with path normalization

Paths containing a parent-directory component with a backslash, like , call into a helper that allocates a temporary heap buffer of 0x301 bytes. Our path is copied in, but it can be larger than the buffer, causing a buffer overflow. lol

We’ll need a good victim allocation to overflow into. Codex found that the object allocates a cache entry for its files. If that entry has its dirty bit set, reads and writes to the file follow a pointer to cached data. We can hijack that for arbitrary read/write.

From here, I scanned through memory to find SmileBASIC’s connection object and set the saved PID to 1. Now, my process has “FullPermission”, meaning I can perform privileged filesystem actions. I dumped internal storage and all ordinary sysmodule code, so Codex could perform offline analysis and I could understand where to go next.

Homebrew and modding typically rely on executing our own native code. Looking at the dumps, the only ordinary sysmodule with permission to map executable code is . All these sysmodules have CFI, PAC, and XOM. The interface for the module seems pretty minimal too. It seemed more fruitful to pursue a logic bug than to look for memory corruption in directly.

Let’s revisit that first point about serving decrypted code. This was useful for dumping the code for ordinary sysmodules. What’s the intended functionality of this interface? Loading programs?

Games and ordinary sysmodules are distributed as Nintendo Content Archives, or NCAs, containing a filesystem image called ExeFS. This contains a file for the main executable, , and program metadata, .

To load a program, the built-in sysmodule asks to open ExeFS, and replies with an IPC handle to the filesystem. also provides two pieces of cryptographic information about the NCA header: the header’s SHA-256 hash and the developer’s signature of that hash. The loader uses this information to perform two signature checks:

  • Is Nintendo’s signature of ’s process permissions and the developer’s public key valid?
  • Is the developer’s signature of the NCA header hash valid?

Seems cryptographically sound to me, because, in theory:

  • the NPDM signature fixes the process permissions and developer key;
  • the key fixes the NCA header’s signature;
  • the signature fixes the NCA header’s hash;
  • the hash fixes the NCA header’s contents, including its filesystem hashes;
  • those hashes fix the executable content.

In practice, however, I’m doubtful of that last claim, because it’s the responsibility of the module to ensure the served filesystem matches the NCA header’s filesystem hash, and we have ARW in it.

Arbitrary r/w to native code execution

Indeed, with ARW, we can replace the ExeFS object behind the loader’s IPC handle with our own temporary filesystem. This filesystem still needs to serve a valid developer for the loader’s first check, but the executable itself can be arbitrary. The second check will pass because, by the time the loader opens the filesystem, has already submitted the valid NCA header hash and signature for the original filesystem.

There are two writes we perform:

  • The first puts a temporary filesystem object we’ve made into the domain-table entry for the loader’s ExeFS. This temporary filesystem contains the original and our replacement .
  • The second puts the loader’s ExeFS object into the domain-table entry for our temporary filesystem. It’s just to keep refcounts consistent and prevent from crashing.

These writes must happen after the loader requests the ExeFS filesystem but before processes the subsequent file requests. How do we ensure this?

The process maintains a list of its IPC connections. When a connection has a new IPC message, processes it. Using our arbitrary read/write, we can replace the handle waits on for the loader’s IPC connection with an event handle we control from SmileBASIC. That lets us control when processes a loader message.

With this, we can execute arbitrary code as any program we have a for!

Getting built-in sysmodule native code execution

What s do we have? Well, all of them. With ARW, we can use to the loader’s connection to copy the NPDM of any ordinary sysmodule or game.

We’ll use this capability to launch our own code using ’s NPDM. As mentioned earlier, ’s NPDM gives it permission to invoke kernel SVCs like SetProcessMemoryPermission, , and . In this case, we’ll use to create a writeable view of ’s existing code. We can also dump ’s code by reading this view.

These calls, however, require a handle to the process. To get a handle to , we’ll use our ARW to overwrite ’s 4-byte handle with and then call from SmileBASIC. The kernel interprets this value to mean “the current process’s handle”, so SmileBASIC gets ’s handle.

We can then send this handle to our custom process, who patches ’s code.

Arbitrary code execution with any ordinary sysmodule’s permissions seems really powerful. We can investigate hardware without first exploiting each device’s driver. I’m hopeful this will help the homebrew community make progress toward CFW.

In the short term, there are a few next steps I think would be interesting:

  • Porting the sysmodule exploit to WebKit. Now that we know what bug we want to exploit, being able to perform arbitrary IPC calls is not as valuable. We might be able to trigger ARW in by changing the data used by WebKit’s existing filesystem code.
  • This jailbreak is tethered, and we don’t currently have a way to compromise built-in sysmodules other than . is a built-in sysmodule, so SM skips service ACL checks from , providing the same capabilities as smhax. I wonder if we can find bugs in other built-in modules?
  • With native code execution in , we can orchestrate its crypto hardware directly. For example, it’s used for NCA4 decryption.
  • The exploit has also been tested on the Switch 1, but I haven’t gotten around to packaging it yet. It wouldn’t provide the capabilities of a modchip, but it wouldn’t require any external hardware.

For now, I’m excited to see all the upcoming Switch 2 homebrew, emulation, and modding.
